title: The Babel Routing Protocol
summary: Defines Babel, a distance-vector routing protocol that avoids loops and works well in both wired networks and wireless mesh networks. It is an experimental protocol and was replaced by RFC 8966.

eli5.summary: Babel is a way for routers to tell neighbors which roads lead where and quickly switch when a road breaks, without driving in circles.

questions: what is the babel routing protocol
how does babel avoid routing loops
what is the babel feasibility condition
subtitle: A distance-vector routing protocol that stays loop-free while networks, wired or wireless, keep changing.

tldr.problem: Classic distance-vector protocols such as RIP can form routing loops and black-holes while they reconverge, which hurts badly in unstable networks like wireless meshes.
tldr.mechanism: Babel only accepts a route update when it can prove the update cannot cause a loop (the feasibility condition), and it uses sequence numbers and explicit requests to recover when no feasible route is left.
tldr.outcome: The result is a protocol that is loop-free in the normal case and quick to reconverge. RFC 6126 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 8966.

today: RFC 6126 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 8966, which is the current definition of Babel. It was also updated by RFC 7298 and RFC 7557.

sections.title: What Babel Is For
sections.content:
Babel is a loop-avoiding distance-vector routing protocol meant to work well both in ordinary wired networks and in wireless mesh networks. Unlike naive distance-vector protocols such as RIP, it strongly limits how often and for how long routing loops and black-holes appear while the network reconverges.

Babel has provisions for link quality estimation and for fairly arbitrary metrics, so it can do plain shortest-path routing or use a metric based on measured packet loss. Nodes can even run with different timing parameters and still form an association. It is a hybrid protocol: it can carry routes for both IPv4 and IPv6, whichever of the two the Babel packets travel over.

The RFC is open about two limitations. Babel sends periodic updates instead of using a reliable transport, so in large stable networks it generates more traffic than OSPF, IS-IS or EIGRP. And it imposes a hold time when a prefix is retracted, which makes it unsuitable for mobile networks that do automatic prefix aggregation.
sections.eli5: Babel is a map-sharing game for routers that is made for places where roads keep closing, like a wireless network. Its main trick is to never believe a tip that might send traffic in a circle.

sections.title: Feasibility and Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
Babel is based on the Bellman-Ford algorithm, like RIP. Each node keeps a distance to a source and a next hop, and neighbours exchange route updates. The weakness of naive Bellman-Ford is that a topology change can cause transient loops, with metrics climbing until they reach infinity.

Babel discards received route announcements unless it can prove that accepting them cannot cause a loop. Its feasibility condition works with the feasibility distance FD(A), the smallest metric that node A has ever advertised for a source. An update from neighbour B is feasible when the metric B advertises is strictly smaller than FD(A). This is the condition used in EIGRP, and the RFC shows it is less restrictive than the simpler condition used by DSDV.

The catch is starvation: a node can run out of feasible routes even though a usable path exists. Babel handles this with sequenced routes. Each route carries a sequence number that only the source increments, and a distance is a pair of sequence number and metric. An update is feasible if its sequence number is newer, or equal with a strictly smaller metric. When a node is starved it sends an explicit request toward the source asking for a new sequence number. The request is forwarded hop by hop with no regard to feasibility, and duplicate detection keeps it from looping.

When several routers originate the same prefix, feasibility distances are kept per source, a pair of router-id and prefix. In that case Babel may create a transient loop, but it disappears in time proportional to its diameter and the routers involved do not take part in such a loop again. Overlapping prefixes are handled by keeping an unreachable route for a few minutes after a retraction, so a node does not fall back to a shorter covering prefix too early.

Sequence numbers decide feasibility, but a node normally ignores them when choosing which route to use.
sections.eli5: A router only trusts a tip if the new road is clearly shorter than anything it has already promised. If it runs out of trusted roads, it asks the destination to send a fresh, newer message so it can start trusting again.

sections.title: How a Babel Node Works
sections.content:
Every speaker has a router-id, an arbitrary string of 8 octets assumed unique in the routing domain, and keeps an interface table, a neighbour table, a source table, a route table and a table of pending requests. Its own sequence number is 16 bits and it should not increase it spontaneously, only in answer to a request for a newer one.

Neighbours are found with periodic Hello messages carrying an increasing sequence number and an interval. A node answers what it hears with IHU (I Heard You) messages, which carry its reception cost for that link. The link cost is local policy, but it must be strictly positive and must be infinite when no Hellos were received recently or the transmission cost is infinite. The route metric function must be strictly monotonic, and should be isotonic.

A received update is checked against the feasibility condition. An unfeasible update is ignored, or treated as a retraction when it replaces an installed route from a different router-id. Route selection is flexible, but it must never choose a retracted or unfeasible route. A simple strategy is to choose the feasible route with the smallest metric, with some hysteresis.

Nodes send periodic full updates, which can be infrequent because Babel relies heavily on triggered updates. A triggered update MUST be sent in a timely manner when the selected router-id for a destination changes, since that may signal a loop forming. Route requests ask for an update on a prefix and are never forwarded. Seqno requests are forwarded to a single neighbour, never multicast, and carry a hop count. A node that has lost all feasible routes to a destination MUST send a seqno request. Nodes may also request acknowledgements, which are always sent as unicast.
sections.eli5: Routers keep saying hello, and answer with I heard you, so each one knows which neighbors are really there and how good each link is. Then they swap route news, and send extra news right away when something important changes.

sections.title: Packets and TLVs
sections.content:
A Babel packet is the body of a UDP datagram, sent with a network-layer hop count of 1 to a well-known multicast address or to a unicast address, over IPv4 or IPv6 (link-local in the IPv6 case). A packet starts with a 4-octet header: a Magic octet with the value 42, a Version octet with the value 2, and a 16-bit body length. Packets with a different magic or version MUST be silently ignored, and any data after the declared body MUST be ignored too.

The body is a sequence of TLVs (type, length, value). Pad1 is a single octet; every other TLV has a type and a length octet followed by the body. TLVs of unknown type, and extra data beyond a TLV's expected length, are silently ignored, which leaves room for extension. Times are 16-bit values in centiseconds, covering up to roughly 11 minutes.

The defined TLVs cover padding, acknowledgement requests and acknowledgements, Hello, IHU, Router-Id, Next Hop, Update, Route Request and Seqno Request. Addresses use encodings AE 0 (wildcard), AE 1 (IPv4), AE 2 (IPv6) and AE 3 (link-local IPv6), and prefixes are stored in the smallest number of octets that hold the significant bits. To save space, an Update can omit the start of its prefix, copying it from an earlier Update in the same packet, and the router-id and next hop come from separate TLVs.

IANA registered UDP port 6697 (called babel), the IPv6 multicast group ff02:0:0:0:0:0:1:6 and the IPv4 multicast group 224.0.0.111. Packets MUST NOT be sent larger than the interface MTU (adjusted for lower-layer headers) or 512 octets, whichever is larger.
sections.eli5: Every Babel message starts with a secret handshake number, 42, so routers can tell it is really Babel. After that come small labeled notes, and a router just skips any note it does not understand.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC states plainly that, as defined, Babel is a completely insecure protocol. Any attacker can attract data traffic by advertising routes with a low metric. The suggested fixes are lower-layer security such as IPsec or link-layer security, or appending a cryptographic key to Babel packets; the rule that data beyond the declared body length is ignored was designed for just that.

Routing information can also reveal a mobile node's physical location with reasonable precision. Using randomly chosen router-ids and IP addresses, changed periodically, mitigates this somewhat. Over IPv6, packets from anything other than a link-local source are ignored, which protects against spoofed packets from the global Internet. No such natural protection exists over IPv4.
sections.eli5: Babel trusts everyone who talks to it, so a sneaky router could lie about having a great shortcut. The fix is to lock the conversation with extra security from outside Babel.

fields.name: Magic
fields.desc: Always 42 (decimal); other first octets are ignored.

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: Version 2 of the protocol; other values are ignored.

fields.name: Body length
fields.desc: Length in octets of the body that follows the header.

items.label: Acknowledgement Request
items.desc: Asks the receiver to acknowledge within an interval.

items.label: Acknowledgement
items.desc: Echoes the nonce of a request; sent to a unicast address.

items.label: Hello
items.desc: Neighbour discovery and link reception cost.

items.label: IHU
items.desc: I Heard You: confirms two-way reachability and carries rxcost.

items.label: Router-Id
items.desc: Sets the router-id implied by later Updates.

items.label: Next Hop
items.desc: Sets the next-hop address for later Updates.

items.label: Route Request
items.desc: Asks for an update for a prefix, or a full table dump.

items.label: Seqno Request
items.desc: Asks for an update with a given sequence number; may be forwarded.
